bet.dominantBottleneck: The dominant bottleneck is manufacturable reproducibility: the demonstrated solid-state transistor effect is real but each device is hand-made, highly variable, and sensitive to surface contamination, so the critical unknown is whether any fabrication strategy can yield consistent, adequately reliable devices in volume at a system-level cost that beats vacuum tubes. Device-to-device variation, not raw gain, is what decides whether this becomes a platform.

routes.route: Pursue junction-transistor refinement on grown/bonded germanium crystals with emphasis on reducing surface-state sensitivity through passivation and hermetic encapsulation.
routes.reason: Junction theory predicts more robust bulk behavior than point-contact, and existing crystal-growing capability plus hermetic packaging addresses the known surface-contamination weakness; this is the lowest-variance path to reproducible discrete devices.

routes.route: Hunt for a surface-stabilized geometry by systematic design-of-experiments over cleaning, etching, ambient gas and bias, mapping which surface treatments reproducibly pin or fix device parameters across many samples.
routes.reason: Since surface effects provably change behavior and are the biggest source of device-to-device spread, a controlled empirical map of surface conditions is cheap, high-information, and could turn an unstable effect into a stable one before any more complex platform work.

routes.route: Develop diffusion and photo-masking batch processing for junction formation, betting that integrated circuit fabrication will amortize over many devices even at low per-wafer yield.
routes.reason: The techniques are plausible but unproven at the circuit level; they only repay if yield and reliability beat discrete assembly, which is not yet demonstrated, so they are worth pursuing in parallel but not as the primary near-term platform.

routes.route: Invest in a systems-level redesign that accepts transistor variability by using redundant or self-compensating circuit topologies tolerant of device spread, enabling discrete transistors to be used before yield improves.
routes.reason: Constraints make clear that variation and yield matter as much as single-device performance; designing circuits that absorb parameter spread could unlock near-term military/space systems and generate revenue and learning to fund process improvement.

routes.route: Pursue a planar surface-protected geometry where the active junction is formed under a protective oxide or masked layer at the surface, testing whether surface stability can be built in rather than sealed in afterwards.
routes.reason: This directly confronts the contamination bottleneck and promises batch manufacturability, but requires the still-unproven diffusion/masking stack to converge, so it should be advanced as a focused research line while discrete reproducibility is secured.

bet.dominantBottleneck: The dominant bottleneck is converting a demonstrated single-device solid-state amplifying effect into a reproducible, high-yield batch fabrication platform—overcoming device-to-device variation, surface contamination instability, and interconnection/reliability burdens—so that economic viability extends beyond a laboratory curiosity into a systems-level electronics platform.

routes.route: Pursue junction-device refinement: focus on growing/purifying single-crystal semiconductor junctions with controlled doping profiles to achieve predictable electrical characteristics, then package them as discrete replacements for point-contact devices.
routes.reason: Junction theory is credible and early junction transistors suggest more robust structures; single-device reliability is the most proximal blocker, and crystal growth/doping is improving, so this route attacks the fundamental physics bottleneck directly.

routes.route: Pursue surface passivation and contamination control as the master variable: systematically characterize how surface states, oxide layers, and adsorbed contaminants shift device behavior, and engineer protective surface treatments before investing further in device geometry.
routes.reason: Surface effects demonstrably change behavior and are unresolved; every other route—junction or planar—fails if surfaces drift, making this a cheap, high-information prerequisite and possibly the true critical path.

routes.route: Pursue photographic masking + diffusion as a batch planar process: develop a mask-based selective doping/etching flow to fabricate many devices on a single wafer, betting that per-wafer cost and interconnection benefits will outweigh early yield losses.
routes.reason: Photographic masking and diffusion are plausible but no proven batch platform exists, and device-to-device variation is a stated constraint; this route carries high near-term yield risk and should wait until single-device fabrication and surface control are stable enough to make batch variation meaningful.

routes.route: Pursue circuit-level integration via hybrid assembly: design modular sub-circuit building blocks (e.g., flip-flops, amplifiers) using the best available discrete devices with printed/embedded wiring to attack the interconnection bottleneck while device fabrication matures.
routes.reason: Complex systems fail on wiring, assembly and reliability even when individual devices work; tackling the interconnection layer in parallel buys system-level value now and informs what a future integrated platform must deliver.

routes.route: Pursue materials-first purity scaling: invest primarily in refined/purified semiconductor ingot growth and metrology to guarantee uniform starting material, treating yield as fundamentally a materials-statistics problem rather than a process problem.
routes.reason: High-purity material is hard but improving, and device-to-device variation is called out as a deciding constraint; superior starting material correctness may subsume later process complexity and pairwise compensate other routes.

routes.route: Pursue yield-engineering via statistical process control: instrument every fabrication step with measurements (resistivity, junction depth, leakage) and feed data back into process tolerances before committing to any full-circuit platform, treating variation as the enemy to be mapped first.
routes.reason: The constraints explicitly rank device-to-device variation and yield as co-equal with single-device performance; a disciplined statistical baseline is cheap, high-information, and de-risks every other route by exposing which step dominates variance.

bet.nextDiscriminatingTest: Build a controlled experiment measuring the same junction device's electrical characteristics (gain, leakage, threshold) under a matrix of surface conditions: freshly etched, oxidized, contaminated, and passivated—across multiple devices from one ingot to separate surface-induced variance from material variance, and establish whether surface stabilization can hold gain and leakage within a spec over days of operation.

bet.dominantBottleneck: Scaling from a validated field-trial formulation to consistent, safe mass manufacture: the trial proves the injected inactivated vaccine prevents paralytic disease in a population, but industrial-scale production must preserve antigenic potency while achieving complete viral inactivation across many independent lots, and no mass campaign has yet stress-tested the full production system.

routes.route: Immediate mass manufacture with lot-release testing, accepting residual risk of rare inactivation failures to accelerate deployment
routes.reason: Trial efficacy does not establish factory reproducibility; releasing millions of doses on batch tests designed for process validation, not yet proven at industrial scale, risks a rare but catastrophic failure that could sicken many recipients and undermine the whole program.

routes.route: Strengthen inactivation process control and lot-release testing before large-scale rollout, using redundant kill steps and enhanced live-virus assays on every lot
routes.reason: This directly targets the dominant bottleneck: complete inactivation across scale. Redundant inactivation steps and more sensitive live-virus detection lower the probability of a rare manufacturing failure without abandoning the proven inactivated formulation.

routes.route: Pursue the live-attenuated oral route as a parallel hedge with separate advantages (ease of administration, stronger mucosal immunity) while the inactivated program scales
routes.reason: The oral route is at an earlier stage and not yet licensed domestically, but it offers a materially different biology that could reduce dependence on the inactivation bottleneck and diversify the public-health portfolio if the injected program hits manufacturing problems.

routes.route: Enhance post-licensure surveillance with careful differentiation of background disease from vaccine-associated cases before mass deployment
routes.reason: Without a surveillance system able to distinguish vaccine-associated paralysis from background disease, a rare failure could be misattributed or missed, corrupting both safety assessment and future trial/epidemiological inference.

routes.route: Conduct a sequential/campaign-like manufacturing and exposure ramp where independent lots are released in stages with aggressive monitoring, pausing if failure signals appear
routes.reason: A staged ramp balances the disease cost of delay against catastrophic failure risk, but the pressure and the lack of any prior mass-campaign evidence make pausing rules politically and operationally fragile; it is better as an operational tactic within a strengthened-process-control route than as a standalone decision.

bet.dominantBottleneck: The decisive bottleneck is temporal attribution: we have spatial patterns (linear magnetic anomalies, ridge morphology, earthquake belts) but no settled way to convert them into a dated kinematic history. Both mobile-floor and fixed-crust models can post-hoc describe the same spatial maps; only something that carries an independent time axis (magnetic reversals sequenced against known ages, sediment age away from ridges, fault-mechanism senses) can discriminate whether the pattern is generated by horizontal crustal motion or by vertical/static crustal processes. Until spatial structure is tied to time, the seafloor-spreading hypothesis remains one flexible narrative among several.

routes.route: Correlate marine magnetic anomaly widths/sequences against the independently dated continental paleomagnetic reversal timescale, predicting symmetric matched-age stripes flanking ridges and increasing age with distance from the axis.
routes.reason: This uniquely couples the spatial linear anomalies to an external dated clock from continental paleomagnetism, so a match both dates the seafloor and discriminates symmetric spreading from static-crust explanations. High information per measurement despite sparse ship tracks.

routes.route: Depth-date the sediment column immediately above oceanic basement at many points across a ridge flank, predicting monotonically increasing basement age with distance from the axis (older away, youngest at the rift), contradicting a fixed-crust model that predicts no systematic age gradient.
routes.reason: Sediment overburden provides an independent age proxy for the underlying crust. A clean monotonic age-distance gradient would be very hard for a static-crust model to reproduce post-hoc and is directly testable from coring on existing bathymetric cruises.

routes.route: Measure focused seismic focal-mechanism and first-motion patterns to test whether ridge earthquakes are extensional (normal faulting) and trench earthquakes are compressional (thrust), as the moving-floor stress regime predicts, versus a fixed-crust model's expectation of mixed or vertical-only mechanisms.
routes.reason: This tests the mechanism implied by horizontal motion rather than its spatial geometry alone. Even a few clean first-motion solutions at a ridge and a trench would break the symmetry between competing kinematic narratives.

routes.route: Map the global pattern of ridge crest to oceanic trench morphology and seafloor depth going from ridge to trench, testing whether predictable subsidence and structure accompany crust aging as required by thermal contraction of newly generated crust spreading outward.
routes.reason: Depth-versus-age relationships are suggestive but currently too under-sampled and confounded by sediment and isostatic unknowns to give a clean discriminator early on; better placed after the time axis is secured from routes one and two.

routes.route: Quantify heat-flow at ridge crests versus flanks expecting high axial values decaying outward, a direct physical consequence of newly emplaced hot crust translating away, versus near-uniform values for a static conductive crust.
routes.reason: Theoretical and instrumental difficulty makes early heat-flow data noisy and sparse; it is a useful later co-confirmation but not the cheapest early discriminator once the chronological signature is being established.

routes.route: Determine from continental paleomagnetic polar-wander paths whether relative motion between continents is ongoing or had a specific onset, comparing the required plate kinematic style against what a symmetric-accretion ridge model predicts globally.
routes.reason: This tests continental motion coherence but is downstream: it presupposes the marine time axis and ridge mechanism resolved, and continental pole paths alone cannot prove seafloor motion without the marine record.

bet.topRoute: Correlate marine magnetic anomaly widths/sequences against the independently dated continental paleomagnetic reversal timescale, predicting symmetric matched-age stripes flanking ridges and increasing age with distance from the axis.
bet.nextDiscriminatingTest: On a well-surveyed, north-south-trending ridge segment already mapped by echo sounding, run a single wide east-west track perpendicular to the ridge collecting continuous magnetometer, depth, and heat-flow readings, and take several short piston cores at regular distance intervals away from the axis. Test the sharp prediction that a bilateral mirror-symmetric anomaly sequence appears about the ridge axis and that the reversal-sequence fit (pinned to continental dated reversals) maps to strictly increasing basement age with distance; a fixed-crust model predicts no bilateral symmetry in anomaly sequence and no monotonic age gradient, so a single clean profile is a high-information discriminating experiment.
requiredComplements: continental paleomagnetic reversal timescale with K-Ar dates
ship-based total-field magnetometer with giro/commutated towed sensor
piston corer with microfossil biostratigraphy for basement age
precision depth recorder tied to the track line
earthquake first-motion/focal-mechanism analysis capability
heat-flow probe lowered through the sediment column
cooperative multi-institution cruise scheduling across a ridge segment
mainFailureRisks: magnetic anomalies may be generated by non-vertical or variable magnetization whose pattern does not map cleanly to reversal timing, invalidating the correlation
repeated reversals of similar duration may produce ambiguity in matching anomaly sequence to the dated reversal record
ship-track navigation errors and sparse coverage may smear the predicted bilateral symmetry
sediment cores may be too short or hiatus-bearing to give genuine basement-age gradients

fixed-crust advocates may respond by adding ad-hoc magnetization sources, making the test degenerate without a second independent observable
bet.generalizationBoundary: A confirmed symmetric age-flanking anomaly correlation near one ridge segment only generalizes as far as that ridge's local spreading regime; it licenses a global marine-reversal timescale only if repeat profiles on several ridge segments at different orientations and latitudes converge on the same reversal chronology and the same monotonic age-distance law. It does not by itself establish continental drift rates, subduction rates at trenches, or the driving mechanism (thermal mantle convection, ridge push, slab pull), all of which require separate kinematic and dynamical constraints. The finding would falsify purely static-crust accounts of that ridge but says nothing directly about regions lacking linear anomalies or about trench or transform-fault kinematics.
unresolvedUnknowns: the exact duration and fine structure of the reversal timescale being used to fit anomalies
whether linear anomalies are caused by symmetric seafloor magnetization or by lateral magnetization contrasts unrelated to age
the role of transform faults and fracture zones in segmenting the anomaly record
whether ridge-normal ship tracks can be navigated precisely enough to guarantee reliable bilateral symmetry tests
the thermal and isostatic state of newly formed crust that controls subsidence and heat flow
the sense and mechanism of deformation at trenches required to complete the kinematic circuit
whether continental polar-wander paths and marine spreading rates can be joined into a single internally consistent global solution
bet.capabilityComplianceNote: All proposed routes, tests, and complements are built strictly from the stated pre-outcome evidence packet (echo sounding, marine magnetometer linear anomalies, continental paleomagnetic reversals, the seafloor-spreading hypothesis, and sparse oceanographic observations). No use is made of any later plate-tectonic synthesis, magnetic-reversal stripe acceptance, or named future instrumentation/institutions beyond what was available at the frontier, and the central test is designed as a genuinely discriminating comparison between mobile-ocean-floor and fixed-crust alternatives rather than a retroactive confirmation.

bet.dominantBottleneck: The dominant bottleneck is the absence of a decisive, high-information observation that distinguishes active seafloor spreading (mobile crust generated at ridges with recorded magnetic history) from fixed-crust alternatives that reinterpret the same anomalies, heat-flow, sediment, and earthquake data as static structures. Sparse, expensive ship time forces choice of discriminating tests.

routes.route: Test whether magnetic anomaly amplitudes decay symmetrically away from ridge axes and whether they correlate with known reversal ages dated from continental lava sequences, implying crustal-age ordering.
routes.reason: This directly confronts the temporal meaning of anomalies: if amplitude falls and pattern matches reversal chronology progressively outward, it argues for recording of reversals during spreading rather than static basement.

routes.route: Measure sediment thickness as a function of distance from ridges to test prediction that sediment accumulates thin at the axis and thickens outward with age, contradicting uniform static basement thickness.
routes.reason: A monotonic sediment-thickness gradient away from ridges is a rate-sensitive prediction of spreading; fixed-crust models must invoke coincidental drainage or basin patterns difficult to defend.

routes.route: Use earthquake epicenter locations and focal mechanisms along ridge-transform systems plus heat-flow profiles across ridge axes to test whether earthquakes concentrate at transform offsets with strike-slip motion as predicted by rigid-plate kinematics.
routes.reason: This tests the geometric self-consistency of moving plates (transform faulting orthogonal to ridge) that a static ridge hypothesis does not naturally produce at the observed constellation of offsets.

routes.route: Link continental paleomagnetic apparent-polar-wander paths to ocean-floor magnetic stripes via reversal chronology, so onshore reversals and offshore anomalies must share a single global time scale.
routes.reason: A shared time scale puts continental and oceanic magnetic records under one budget, forcing the two datasets into a mutual constraint that protects against each being flexibly adjusted in isolation.

routes.route: Test whether crustal ages implied by anomaly spacing increase monotonically to maximum ages at trench boundaries, and whether trenches consume crust at rates consistent with global spreading mass balance.
routes.reason: Mass-balance closure across trenches is logically compelling but currently too assumption-heavy (unknown subduction rates, uncertain convergence) to discriminate cleanly; it is a complement to be checked after the reversal-time-scale route yields dated ages.

routes.route: Model whether fixed-crust alternatives can reproduce all these observations (sediment gradient, symmetric anomalies, transform seismicity, heat-flow) with a single flexible mechanism, versus the spreading model's one mechanism for many predictions.
routes.reason: Comparing model parsimony and falsifiability is a legitimate route because the pressure explicitly demands distinguishing predictive moving-floor claims from post-hoc fixed-crust fixes; a single-mechanism account is favored if it covers more independent predictions.

bet.topRoute: Test whether magnetic anomaly amplitudes decay symmetrically away from ridge axes and whether they correlate with known reversal ages dated from continental lava sequences, implying crustal-age ordering.
bet.nextDiscriminatingTest: The highest-information, cheapest discriminating test is to run a focused survey along a single mid-ocean ridge flank: measure magnetic anomaly amplitude and polarity sequence with a shipboard magnetometer, and simultaneously sample the oldest continental lava sequences with known paleomagnetic reversal chronology and K-Ar dating. If the offshore anomaly sequence matches the onshore reversal sequence in both polarity order and relative spacing, and amplitudes decay monotonically with distance from the axis, then the mobile-spreading interpretation is strongly supported against fixed-crust reinterpretation, at moderate cost concentrated on one transect with complementary onshore dating.

Any claim of a global synthesis must therefore be restricted to the correlation of dated reversal sequences with symmetric ridge-flank anomalies, and must separately extend to trenches and continental motion.

bet.dominantBottleneck: The dominant bottleneck is orbital rendezvous/docking reliability as the enabling technology: all viable architectures that fit the Saturn-family mass ceiling require at least one in-space mating event, yet crewed rendezvous, docking and deep-space precision navigation are unproven capabilities whose failure risk must force the whole-system trade between launcher payoff and added mission complexity.

routes.route: Direct ascent: build a very large launch vehicle/spacecraft (or a small family of launches) to place the entire landed-and-return stack on the lunar surface in one go, avoiding any orbital assembly or lunar-orbit mating.
routes.reason: Mass constraints make a single-vehicle direct landing infeasible with the Saturn family under the deadline; it survives only as a fallback if Earth-orbit assembly proves too slow, but the required launcher growth is itself off critical path.

routes.route: Earth-orbit rendezvous: several Saturn launches assemble and refuel a trans-lunar stack in low Earth orbit before a single integrated departure, using rendezvous/docking proved in Earth orbit where abort is feasible.
routes.reason: It confines all new rendezvous risk to near-Earth where crew abort and return are routine, gives schedule slack by decoupling launcher readiness from the landing stack, and incrementally validates docking before committing to the Moon.

routes.route: Lunar-orbit rendezvous (LOR): one launch places a small landing module at the Moon while a command/service module remains in lunar orbit to recover the ascent stage, minimizing landed and lunar-liftoff mass.
routes.reason: LOR cuts lunar-landed and lunar-ascent mass most sharply against the hard launch-mass ceiling, repaying the added complexity at whole-system level; the offsetting cost is a demanding lunar-orbit rendezvous that needs staged Earth-orbit proof first.

routes.route: Combined EOR-plus-LOR: assemble fuel and stack in Earth orbit and also separate a landing module in lunar orbit, spreading mass demand across both assembly arenas.
routes.reason: It minimizes peak single-launch mass but double-counts rendezvous risk in two arenas, increasing validation burden and the number of unproven crewed mating events beyond what the schedule can safely absorb.

routes.route: Fuel/refueling depots in Earth orbit allowing many small launches to top off a reusable trans-lunar stack rather than one large assembly.
routes.reason: Unproven cryogenic storage and in-space transfer add lifecycle and schedule risk that dwarfs their modest mass advantage; it needs EOR docking proven first and does not relax the lunar descent/ascent mass demand that LOR targets.

routes.route: Test-as-you-go staged validation: prove crewed rendezvous/docking in progressively higher energy regimes (LEO, high Earth orbit, lunar orbit abort demonstrations) before committing the architecture's critical mating events.
routes.reason: This is not a competing architecture but the precondition for whichever mating route is chosen; it converts the largest unknown (unproven rendezvous) into measured risk and gates the LOR vs EOR decision on data.

bet.topRoute: Lunar-orbit rendezvous (LOR): one launch places a small landing module at the Moon while a command/service module remains in lunar orbit to recover the ascent stage, minimizing landed and lunar-liftoff mass.
bet.nextDiscriminatingTest: Fly a crewed demonstration mission that performs rendezvous and docking in low Earth orbit with a separately launched target, then repeats the same guidance/navigation/docking sequence in a higher-energy elliptical orbit to prove the deep-space targeting and closing algorithm that lunar-orbit rendezvous depends on, while logging per-mission rendezvous success, propellant margins and abort windows to weigh LOR's mass payoff against measured docking risk versus EOR's schedule slack.
